idiom_name: one guardian object owning the lock and the state, every access through its guarded operations
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: create one object per invariant that owns (a) the mutable state and (b) the synchronisation primitive that serialises access to it, and make every operation a method of that object which acquires the primitive, performs the whole read-modify-write, and releases on every path. Keep the state unreachable from outside - no public field, no returned collection, no iterator or reference escaping the critical section; operations that need a compound view return a copy or compute under the lock. Choose the primitive inside the object (blocking vs suspending, plain vs recursive, exclusive vs read-write, lock vs atomic) so callers never see it, and keep the critical section short and free of callbacks, blocking I/O and calls into other guarded objects. The design is only as strong as the language allows: where the type system can express 'state only reachable with the lock' (a mutex that owns its data, actor isolation), prefer that form over convention; where it cannot, the encapsulation is a documented invariant of the module and the object must be the only route to the state.
pitfalls: Leaving the state publishable (public field, returned collection, iterator, reference into the guarded structure) gives callers a path around the lock that no test will notice.
Doing slow or re-entrant work while holding the lock - formatting, logging, I/O, invoking a callback - turns the serialisation point into a bottleneck and a deadlock risk.
Guarding only the 'important' operations, so one forgotten accessor still reads or writes the state unsynchronised and the invariant breaks where it matters most.

Synchronising on a non-final lock field: if the lock reference can be reassigned, a thread that acquires the old lock and another that acquires the new lock operate on different serialisation points, leaving the state completely unguarded with no compilation error.

Holding the lock across I/O operations, logging calls, or callbacks: any blocking or re-entrant operation while holding the lock transforms the guardian from a serialisation point into a latency multiplier and a potential deadlock host.

Locking on a publicly accessible object — String intern pool, a class object, another component's monitor — which allows unrelated code to take the same lock and deadlock the guardian's own operations.

Using a re-entrant lock to make self-deadlock 'work': if a guarded method calls another guarded method on the same guardian, the re-entrant lock silently widens the critical section across the entire call graph, masking a design error rather than fixing one.

Unguarded publication of a copy: returning a reference to a field that is a collection or mutable object (even if intended as a snapshot) lets callers mutate the state outside the lock; the fix requires always copying out, never returning references.

Subclass synchronising on the superclass's lock or instance: when a superclass uses the private lock idiom and a subclass synchronises on 'this' or the superclass lock, the two locking policies interfere and produce unpredictable atomicity violations.

Acquiring two guardians' locks in opposite orders from different call sites: a circular lock acquisition across two guardians is a deadlock; document lock ordering or use a meta-lock to break the cycle when multi-guardian operations are unavoidable.

Wrong move: synchronising on 'this', the class object, or an interned String because it is convenient -> untrusted or unrelated code can acquire the same monitor and hold it indefinitely (denial of service, CERT LCK00-J) or already synchronises on that reused object without your knowledge (CERT LCK01-J), and the lock silently becomes part of the class's public contract -> instead use a private final lock object dedicated to this state and block-synchronise on it rather than using synchronised methods.

Wrong move: letting call sites compose two guardians while each holds its own lock, acquiring them in whatever order reads naturally -> the two private locks are taken in opposite orders from different sites and the system deadlocks, with the acquisition order invisible in any single caller because both locks are private (CERT LCK07-J) -> instead fix a global lock-acquisition order, take both with tryLock-and-backoff, or fold the jointly-invariant state into one guardian so a single private lock covers the whole operation.

Wrong move: declaring the lock field non-final so the synchronisation policy can be swapped at runtime -> two threads acquire two different lock instances and serialise nothing, the invariant is lost with no compile error or test failure -> instead keep the lock field private final (final already gives the needed visibility; the lock itself does not need volatile), and if finer granularity is needed, add additional private final lock objects instead of reassigning one.
